images.caption: Figure 1:Overview of the proposed framework.(Top)During training, FWLAug augments FWL samples while preserving ToF waveform structure and frustum geometry. High-intensity patches are selected by pruning, spatially reordered along a space-filling curve, and processed by theFWL-ToPMEncoder, which merges redundant tokens before self-attention and unmerges afterward acrossLLTransformer blocks.(Bottom Left)Pruning removes low-intensity background tokens, and merging aggregates the remainder, concentrating computation on object-relevant waveform content.(Bottom Right)Proportion of pixel classes across intensity bins in FWL data. Most regions in FWL data correspond to noisy background, and our pruning strategy removes these dominant low-intensity regions.

Figure 2:Illustration of FWLAug.FWLShiftMix(top): an object in Sample 1 is shifted away from the LiDAR, creating a blank regionΩblank\Omega_{\mathrm{blank}}. A glass-containing regionΩsrc\Omega_{\mathrm{src}}is then selected from Sample 2 and pasted into the blank, producing an augmented scene in which the waveform structure of each ray is preserved.FWLCutMix(bottom): a crop regionΩsrc\Omega_{\mathrm{src}}containing minority class (glass) is selected from a source frame and pasted into a destination frame at a random location. Both methods prioritize glass-containing regions to mitigate class imbalance.

Figure 4:Visualization of token merging on two real Ghost-FWL scenes. Color indicates patch intensity (red: high, white: low). After pruning low-intensity background tokens, the remaining high-intensity tokens are merged by aggregating similar-feature source tokens into destination tokens, reducing the total token count while preserving object-relevant content. The zoomed-in regions show that merged tokens retain the spatial structure of reflected objects across diverse scenes.

Figure 1:Our OOD Test Set. Based on the dense 3D maps as shown in Scene, we annotated FWL data with 4 labels: Ghost (red), Object (green), Glass (blue), Noise. Blue crosses indicate the LiDAR positions during data acquisition. The RGB images show the scenery of the capture locations.

Figure 2:Waveforms along single rays in Ghost-FWL Scene 001 (left) and Scene 007 (right). Markers indicate annotated Object (green), Glass (blue), and Ghost (red) bins, labels indicate the Top-3 highest-intensity peaks of each ray, and the dashed line indicates the intensity threshold below which patches are pruned atρlow=0.7\rho_{\mathrm{low}}=0.7. The photographs show the corresponding scenes, with the red marker indicating the observed ray. Top-3 peak extraction discards the Object and the Glass return, whereas our intensity-based pruning retains both because they lie above the pruning threshold.
Figure 3:Qualitative comparison of classification results with existing FWL-based recognition methods.
